claim: Up to 70% of parasite-controlled changes in the host transcriptome rely on the MYR1 protein.
source: Up to 70% of parasite-controlled changes in the host transcriptome rely on the MYR1 protein, which is required for the translocation of secreted proteins into the host cell.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work, as indicated by the context of the abstract discussing established findings.

claim: MYR1 is required for the translocation of secreted proteins into the host cell.
source: Up to 70% of parasite-controlled changes in the host transcriptome rely on the MYR1 protein, which is required for the translocation of secreted proteins into the host cell.
evidence: This is an established fact about MYR1 function supported by prior research.

claim: Mice infected with MYR1 knock-out (KO) strains survive infection.
source: Mice infected with MYR1 knock-out (KO) strains survive infection, supporting a paramount function of MYR1-dependent secreted proteins in Toxoplasma virulence and proliferation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior experimental work.

claim: MYR1 mutants have no growth defect in pooled in vivo CRISPR-Cas9 screens in mice.
source: However, we have previously shown that MYR1 mutants have no growth defect in pooled in vivo CRISPR-Cas9 screens in mice, suggesting that the presence of parasites that are wild-type at the myr1 locus in pooled screens can rescue the phenotype.
evidence: This is supported by the authors' previous experimental data.

claim: MYR1 is not required for the survival in IFN-γ-activated murine macrophages.
source: Here, we demonstrate that MYR1 is not required for the survival in IFN-γ-activated murine macrophages, and that parasites lacking MYR1 are able to expand during the onset of infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Parasites lacking MYR1 are able to expand during the onset of infection.
source: Here, we demonstrate that MYR1 is not required for the survival in IFN-γ-activated murine macrophages, and that parasites lacking MYR1 are able to expand during the onset of infection.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: ΔMYR1 parasites have restricted growth in single-strain murine infections.
source: While ΔMYR1 parasites have restricted growth in single-strain murine infections, we show that the phenotype is rescued by co-infection with wild-type (WT) parasites in vivo, independent of host functional adaptive immunity or key pro-inflammatory cytokines.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The growth defect phenotype of ΔMYR1 parasites is rescued by co-infection with wild-type (WT) parasites in vivo.
source: While ΔMYR1 parasites have restricted growth in single-strain murine infections, we show that the phenotype is rescued by co-infection with wild-type (WT) parasites in vivo, independent of host functional adaptive immunity or key pro-inflammatory cytokines.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: The rescue of ΔMYR1 parasites by WT parasites is independent of host functional adaptive immunity.
source: While ΔMYR1 parasites have restricted growth in single-strain murine infections, we show that the phenotype is rescued by co-infection with wild-type (WT) parasites in vivo, independent of host functional adaptive immunity or key pro-inflammatory cytokines.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data using Rag2-deficient mice.

claim: The rescue of ΔMYR1 parasites by WT parasites is independent of key pro-inflammatory cytokines.
source: While ΔMYR1 parasites have restricted growth in single-strain murine infections, we show that the phenotype is rescued by co-infection with wild-type (WT) parasites in vivo, independent of host functional adaptive immunity or key pro-inflammatory cytokines.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing rescue despite high cytokine levels.

claim: The major function of MYR1-dependent secreted proteins is not to protect the parasite from clearance within infected cells.
source: These data show that the major function of MYR1-dependent secreted proteins is not to protect the parasite from clearance within infected cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing MYR1 is not required for survival in IFN-γ-activated macrophages.

claim: MYR-dependent proteins generate a permissive niche in a paracrine manner.
source: Instead, MYR-dependent proteins generate a permissive niche in a paracrine manner, which rescues ΔMYR1 parasites within a pool of CRISPR mutants in mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from co-infection experiments.

claim: MYR-dependent proteins rescue ΔMYR1 parasites within a pool of CRISPR mutants in mice.
source: Instead, MYR-dependent proteins generate a permissive niche in a paracrine manner, which rescues ΔMYR1 parasites within a pool of CRISPR mutants in mice.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data comparing pooled and single-strain infections.

claim: Pooled CRISPR screens have been applied in various cell culture conditions and in vivo.
source: They have been applied in various cell culture conditions and in vivo, in combination with different genetic or chemical bottlenecks to identify genes in a specific setting (Bock et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Fitness-conferring genes are identified by assessing the relative abundance of cells with different genetic perturbations within a pool of mutants upon selective pressure.
source: Fitness-conferring genes are identified by assessing the relative abundance of cells with different genetic perturbations within a pool of mutants upon selective pressure.
evidence: This describes the established methodology of pooled CRISPR screens.

claim: Pooled CRISPR screens have been performed in mice with Toxoplasma gondii to identify exported parasite proteins important for survival in the natural host.
source: We have previously performed pooled CRISPR screens in mice with the intracellular parasite Toxoplasma gondii, to identify exported parasite proteins that are important for survival in his natural host (Young et al., 2019; Butterworth et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: For the majority of tested genes, the phenotypes observed in pooled CRISPR screens are concordant to those observed in single-strain infections using clonal mutants.
source: For the majority of tested genes, the phenotypes observed in pooled CRISPR screens are concordant to those observed in single-strain infections using clonal mutants for those genes.
evidence: This is based on the authors' previous experimental observations.

claim: Some Toxoplasma genes are required for survival in single-strain mutant KO murine infections but show no fitness defect when the same mutants are part of a heterogenous mutant pool used for CRISPR screens in mice.
source: To our surprise, however, we found that while some Toxoplasma genes are required for survival in single-strain mutant KO murine infections, this fitness defect phenotype is lost when the same mutants are part of a heterogenous mutant pool used for CRISPR screens in mice.
evidence: This is based on the authors' experimental observations.

claim: Individual mutants can be rescued by paracrine effects triggered by other parasites in the pool.
source: We hypothesised that individual mutants can be rescued by paracrine effects triggered by other parasites in the pool, pointing towards a potential limitation of pooled CRISPR screens to detect a subset of important virulence factors in Toxoplasma.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the authors' observations.

claim: Paracrine rescue represents a potential limitation of pooled CRISPR screens to detect a subset of important virulence factors in Toxoplasma.
source: We hypothesised that individual mutants can be rescued by paracrine effects triggered by other parasites in the pool, pointing towards a potential limitation of pooled CRISPR screens to detect a subset of important virulence factors in Toxoplasma.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations.

claim: The limitation of pooled CRISPR screens due to paracrine effects is likely not restricted to Toxoplasma or other infectious contexts, but to CRISPR screens in general where paracrine effects are operating.
source: This limitation likely is not restricted to Toxoplasma, or other infectious contexts, but CRISPR screens in general where paracrine effects are operating.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the findings.

claim: Toxoplasma gondii is a ubiquitous parasitic pathogen in all warm-blooded animals.
source: Toxoplasma is a ubiquitous parasitic pathogen in all warm-blooded animals.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Toxoplasma.

claim: Toxoplasma infection is widespread in livestock and wild animals, as well as in humans.
source: Toxoplasma infection is widespread in livestock and wild animals, as well as in humans, where one third of the population is estimated to be seropositive (Pappas et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: One third of the human population is estimated to be seropositive for Toxoplasma.
source: Toxoplasma infection is widespread in livestock and wild animals, as well as in humans, where one third of the population is estimated to be seropositive (Pappas et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Following oral infection by oocysts or latent stage tissue cysts, the parasite grows as tachyzoites in intermediate hosts, before disseminating to distal organs.
source: Following oral infection by oocysts or latent stage tissue cysts, the parasite grows as tachyzoites in intermediate hosts, before disseminating to distal organs.
evidence: This describes the established life cycle of Toxoplasma.

claim: The host immune response is pivotal to reduce parasite burden caused by rapidly proliferating tachyzoites.
source: The host immune response is pivotal to reduce parasite burden caused by rapidly proliferating tachyzoites.
evidence: This is established knowledge about host-parasite interactions.

claim: The host immune response is not sufficient to completely clear Toxoplasma infection.
source: However, it is not sufficient to completely clear infection, as surviving parasites can differentiate into the chronic bradyzoite forms and establish tissue cysts in the central nervous system and skeletal muscle cells (Dubey et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Surviving Toxoplasma parasites can differentiate into chronic bradyzoite forms and establish tissue cysts in the central nervous system and skeletal muscle cells.
source: However, it is not sufficient to completely clear infection, as surviving parasites can differentiate into the chronic bradyzoite forms and establish tissue cysts in the central nervous system and skeletal muscle cells (Dubey et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Recognition of Toxoplasma-derived pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) by host innate immune cells triggers the production of IL-12.
source: During the onset of infection, recognition of Toxoplasma-derived pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) by host innate immune cells triggers the production of IL-12, amongst other pro-inflammatory mediators (Sasai and Yamamoto, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: IL-12 has a protective role during toxoplasmosis, primarily by triggering IFN-γ production in lymphocytes.
source: IL-12 has a protective role during toxoplasmosis, primarily by triggering IFN-γ production in lymphocytes and thereby linking innate and adaptive immunity during infection (Gazzinelli et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: IFN-γ is a pivotal cytokine in conferring resistance against Toxoplasma infection.
source: IFN-γ is a pivotal cytokine in conferring resistance against Toxoplasma infection since it induces expression of interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs) that limit intracellular parasite proliferation and curtail infection (Saeij and Frickel, 2017; MacMicking, 2012; Hunn et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: IFN-γ induces expression of interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs) that limit intracellular parasite proliferation and curtail infection.
source: IFN-γ is a pivotal cytokine in conferring resistance against Toxoplasma infection since it induces expression of interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs) that limit intracellular parasite proliferation and curtail infection (Saeij and Frickel, 2017; MacMicking, 2012; Hunn et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The antimicrobial effects of IFN-γ are enhanced by other pro-inflammatory cytokines.
source: These antimicrobial effects are enhanced by other pro-inflammatory cytokines.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cytokine interactions.

claim: TNF acts as a co-stimulatory signal to trigger IFN-γ production by NK cells exposed to Toxoplasma.
source: An example is TNF, which acts as a co-stimulatory signal to trigger IFN-γ production by NK cells exposed to the parasite, and boosts the antimicrobial activity of IFN-γ-activated macrophages (Sibley et al., 1991; Langermans et al., 1992; Sher et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: TNF boosts the antimicrobial activity of IFN-γ-activated macrophages.
source: An example is TNF, which acts as a co-stimulatory signal to trigger IFN-γ production by NK cells exposed to the parasite, and boosts the antimicrobial activity of IFN-γ-activated macrophages (Sibley et al., 1991; Langermans et al., 1992; Sher et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Following Toxoplasma infection, host cells can secrete chemokines such as CCL2.
source: Following Toxoplasma infection, host cells can also secrete chemokines such as CCL2, which drives recruitment of CCR2+Ly6Chigh inflammatory monocytes from the bone marrow to the infected sites (Robben et al., 2005; Dunay et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: CCL2 drives recruitment of CCR2+Ly6Chigh inflammatory monocytes from the bone marrow to infected sites.
source: Following Toxoplasma infection, host cells can also secrete chemokines such as CCL2, which drives recruitment of CCR2+Ly6Chigh inflammatory monocytes from the bone marrow to the infected sites (Robben et al., 2005; Dunay et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Recruited inflammatory monocytes can differentiate into monocyte-derived dendritic cells or macrophages and act as an extra line of defence against Toxoplasma.
source: There, they can differentiate into monocyte-derived dendritic cells or macrophages and act as an extra line of defence against the parasite (Ruiz-Rosado et al., 2016; Goldszmid et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Toxoplasma relies on an array of over 250 secreted proteins to survive clearance by host immune cells and to disseminate within the infected host.
source: In order to survive clearance by host immune cells and to disseminate within the infected host, Toxoplasma relies on an array of over 250 secreted proteins (Barylyuk et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Following invasion, Toxoplasma replicates inside a parasitophorous vacuole (PV) separated from the host cytoplasm by the PV membrane (PVM).
source: Following invasion, Toxoplasma replicates inside a parasitophorous vacuole (PV) separated from the host cytoplasm by the PV membrane (PVM).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Toxoplasma biology.

claim: During and after host cell invasion, Toxoplasma secretes proteins from the rhoptries and the dense granules.
source: During and after host cell invasion, Toxoplasma secretes proteins from the rhoptries and the dense granules.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Toxoplasma secretion.

claim: Secreted proteins from rhoptries and dense granules are pivotal for vacuole establishment, nutrient uptake, reprogramming of the infected cell and protection against the host immune response.
source: Secreted proteins from these organelles are not only pivotal for vacuole establishment, but also nutrient uptake, reprogramming of the infected cell and protection against the host immune response (Hakimi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Some Toxoplasma proteins secreted from dense granules must cross the PVM, likely via a multi-protein translocon that depends on MYR1.
source: In order to exert their effect, some Toxoplasma proteins secreted from dense granules must cross the PVM, likely via a multi-protein translocon that depends on MYR1 (Franco et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: GRA16 is a dense granule effector that relies on MYR-dependent export to exit the PV and reach the host cytosol.
source: GRA16, a dense granule effector that relies on MYR-dependent export to exit the PV and reach the host cytosol, was shown to drive upregulation of the transcription factor c-Myc in host cells (Panas and Boothroyd, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: GRA16 drives upregulation of the transcription factor c-Myc in host cells.
source: GRA16, a dense granule effector that relies on MYR-dependent export to exit the PV and reach the host cytosol, was shown to drive upregulation of the transcription factor c-Myc in host cells (Panas and Boothroyd, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: MYR2, MYR3, MYR4, and ROP17 are putative components of the MYR translocon.
source: After the identification of MYR1 other putative components of the MYR translocon – MYR2, MYR3, MYR4, ROP17 – were identified, using their ability to trigger GRA16-dependent c-Myc induction in infected cells as a surrogate (Marino et al., 2018; Panas et al., 2019a; Cygan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Most, if not all exported dense granule proteins that reach the host cell cytosol might depend on functional MYR1 for translocation.
source: It was subsequently suggested that most, if not all exported dense granule proteins that reach the host cell cytosol might depend on functional MYR1 for translocation (Panas et al., 2019a; Sangaré et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Seven virulence factors have been shown to be MYR1-dependent: IST, NSM, HCE1/TEEGR, GRA16, GRA18, GRA24, and GRA28.
source: To date, seven virulence factors have been shown to be MYR1-dependent: IST, NSM, HCE1/TEEGR, GRA16, GRA18, GRA24, and GRA28.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: IST boosts resistance against IFN-γ-dependent antimicrobial mechanisms.
source: Examples include boosting resistance against IFN-γ-dependent antimicrobial mechanisms (IST Olias et al., 2016; Gay et al., 2016), arresting the host cell cycle (HCE1/TEEGR Panas et al., 2019b; Braun et al., 2019), inhibiting programmed host cell death pathways (NSM Rosenberg and Sibley, 2021) and modulating cytokine/chemokine secretion (GRA16, GRA18, GRA24, GRA28 Bougdour et al., 2013; He et al., 2018; Braun et al., 2013; Ten Hoeve et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: HCE1/TEEGR arrests the host cell cycle.
source: Examples include boosting resistance against IFN-γ-dependent antimicrobial mechanisms (IST Olias et al., 2016; Gay et al., 2016), arresting the host cell cycle (HCE1/TEEGR Panas et al., 2019b; Braun et al., 2019), inhibiting programmed host cell death pathways (NSM Rosenberg and Sibley, 2021) and modulating cytokine/chemokine secretion (GRA16, GRA18, GRA24, GRA28 Bougdour et al., 2013; He et al., 2018; Braun et al., 2013; Ten Hoeve et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: NSM inhibits programmed host cell death pathways.
source: Examples include boosting resistance against IFN-γ-dependent antimicrobial mechanisms (IST Olias et al., 2016; Gay et al., 2016), arresting the host cell cycle (HCE1/TEEGR Panas et al., 2019b; Braun et al., 2019), inhibiting programmed host cell death pathways (NSM Rosenberg and Sibley, 2021) and modulating cytokine/chemokine secretion (GRA16, GRA18, GRA24, GRA28 Bougdour et al., 2013; He et al., 2018; Braun et al., 2013; Ten Hoeve et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: GRA16, GRA18, GRA24, and GRA28 modulate cytokine/chemokine secretion.
source: Examples include boosting resistance against IFN-γ-dependent antimicrobial mechanisms (IST Olias et al., 2016; Gay et al., 2016), arresting the host cell cycle (HCE1/TEEGR Panas et al., 2019b; Braun et al., 2019), inhibiting programmed host cell death pathways (NSM Rosenberg and Sibley, 2021) and modulating cytokine/chemokine secretion (GRA16, GRA18, GRA24, GRA28 Bougdour et al., 2013; He et al., 2018; Braun et al., 2013; Ten Hoeve et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The vast majority of transcriptional changes in Toxoplasma-infected human fibroblasts are dependent on MYR1.
source: Given the combined importance of exported dense granule effectors, it is not surprising that the vast majority of transcriptional changes in Toxoplasma-infected human fibroblasts are dependent on MYR1 (Naor et al., 2018), and that isogenic MYR1-deficient strains are avirulent in mice (Franco et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Isogenic MYR1-deficient strains are avirulent in mice.
source: Given the combined importance of exported dense granule effectors, it is not surprising that the vast majority of transcriptional changes in Toxoplasma-infected human fibroblasts are dependent on MYR1 (Naor et al., 2018), and that isogenic MYR1-deficient strains are avirulent in mice (Franco et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: In pooled in vivo CRISPR screens, parasites lacking MYR1 had no fitness defect in a five-day infection experiment within the mouse peritoneum.
source: In pooled in vivo CRISPR screens, however, we have shown that parasites lacking MYR1 had no fitness defect in a five-day infection experiment within the mouse peritoneum (Young et al., 2019; Butterworth et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the authors' prior work.

claim: In vivo CRISPR screens performed in other labs using different parasite strains and mouse backgrounds showed no or only very mild growth defects for MYR1.
source: This is in agreement with results from in vivo CRISPR screens performed in other labs using different parasite strains and mouse backgrounds where no (Sangaré et al., 2019; Tachibana et al., 2023), or only very mild growth defects (Giuliano et al., 2024) have been observed for MYR1.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work from other labs.

claim: MYR1, and therefore proteins that rely on the MYR complex for translocation, are not essential for the cell-autonomous survival of parasites in macrophages.
source: This divergence of results between isogenic infection, which clearly shows an important role for MYR1 in murine infections, and the pooled CRISPR screens, which show no defect of MYR1 mutants, led us to hypothesise that: (1) MYR1, and therefore proteins that rely on the MYR complex for translocation, are not essential for the cell-autonomous survival of parasites in macrophages, the main cell type infected in the first days of a peritoneal infection (Jensen et al., 2011); and (2) ΔMYR1 parasites within a pool of mutants may be rescued by MYR1-competent parasites via a paracrine effect, setting up a parasite-permissive immune environment in which MYR1-deficient mutants can thrive.
evidence: This is a hypothesis that is subsequently tested in the manuscript.

claim: Macrophages are the main cell type infected in the first days of a peritoneal Toxoplasma infection.
source: This divergence of results between isogenic infection, which clearly shows an important role for MYR1 in murine infections, and the pooled CRISPR screens, which show no defect of MYR1 mutants, led us to hypothesise that: (1) MYR1, and therefore proteins that rely on the MYR complex for translocation, are not essential for the cell-autonomous survival of parasites in macrophages, the main cell type infected in the first days of a peritoneal infection (Jensen et al., 2011); and (2) ΔMYR1 parasites within a pool of mutants may be rescued by MYR1-competent parasites via a paracrine effect, setting up a parasite-permissive immune environment in which MYR1-deficient mutants can thrive.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: ΔMYR1 parasites within a pool of mutants may be rescued by MYR1-competent parasites via a paracrine effect.
source: This divergence of results between isogenic infection, which clearly shows an important role for MYR1 in murine infections, and the pooled CRISPR screens, which show no defect of MYR1 mutants, led us to hypothesise that: (1) MYR1, and therefore proteins that rely on the MYR complex for translocation, are not essential for the cell-autonomous survival of parasites in macrophages, the main cell type infected in the first days of a peritoneal infection (Jensen et al., 2011); and (2) ΔMYR1 parasites within a pool of mutants may be rescued by MYR1-competent parasites via a paracrine effect, setting up a parasite-permissive immune environment in which MYR1-deficient mutants can thrive.
evidence: This is a hypothesis that is subsequently tested in the manuscript.

claim: GRA12 was shown to be required for parasite survival in IFN-γ-stimulated macrophages.
source: As GRA12 was shown to be required for parasite survival in IFN-γ-stimulated macrophages (Fox et al., 2019) and had a strong growth defect in our pooled in vivo CRISPR screen (Young et al., 2019), we included a ΔGRA12 strain in these experiments as positive control.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: GRA12 had a strong growth defect in pooled in vivo CRISPR screens.
source: As GRA12 was shown to be required for parasite survival in IFN-γ-stimulated macrophages (Fox et al., 2019) and had a strong growth defect in our pooled in vivo CRISPR screen (Young et al., 2019), we included a ΔGRA12 strain in these experiments as positive control.
evidence: This is supported by citation to the authors' prior work.

claim: IST is a known MYR1-dependent factor that inhibits the induction of interferon-stimulated genes.
source: As negative control, we included parasites lacking IST (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), a known MYR1-dependent factor that inhibits the induction of interferon-stimulated genes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about IST function.

claim: IST protects parasites against intracellular restriction when the infection precedes IFN-γ activation, but not if Toxoplasma infects primed cells.
source: IST protects the parasites against intracellular restriction when the infection precedes IFN-γ activation, but not if Toxoplasma infects primed cells (Olias et al., 2016; Gay et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: ΔGRA12 parasites showed a significant reduction in the proportion of infected cells in the presence of IFN-γ.
source: As expected, ΔGRA12 parasites showed a significant reduction in the proportion of infected cells in the presence of IFN-γ (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: Infection with ΔMYR1 was comparable to ΔIST and not significantly different to that of WT parasites in IFN-γ-activated macrophages.
source: Infection with ΔMYR1 was comparable to ΔIST and not significantly different to that of WT parasites, although a slight increase in restriction was observed for ΔIST and ΔMYR1.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Deletion of MYR1 in a type I strain causes no fitness defect in IFN-γ-activated macrophages.
source: Our results are in line with findings from Wang and colleagues where deletion of MYR1 in a more virulent type I strain similarly causes no fitness defect in IFN-γ-activated macrophages (Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: ΔGRA12 was outcompeted by WT parasites exclusively in BMDMs pre-stimulated with IFN-γ.
source: As expected, ΔGRA12 was outcompeted by WT parasites exclusively in BMDMs pre-stimulated with IFN-γ, confirming its role to survive the cytokine-mediated clearance in macrophages (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: ΔMYR1 parasites displayed a fitness defect compared to WT parasites, regardless of the infected cell type and independently of IFN-γ treatment.
source: On the contrary, ΔMYR1 parasites displayed a fitness defect compared to WT parasites, regardless of the infected cell type and independently of IFN-γ treatment (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: ΔMYR1 plaques are smaller in size compared to the parental strain in HFFs.
source: This result is in line with the smaller size of the ΔMYR1 plaques established in HFFs compared to the parental strain (Figure 1d), which recapitulates published data (Marino et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1d and citation to prior work.

claim: ΔMYR1-Luc showed reduced bioluminescent signal compared to WT-Luc parasites in vivo.
source: As expected from the reduced in vitro growth phenotype in HFFs and BMDMs, ΔMYR1-Luc showed reduced bioluminescent signal compared to WT-Luc parasites (Figure 2b and c), confirming that the growth defect in vitro results in analogous phenotypes in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b and c.

claim: The growth defect of ΔMYR1 in vitro results in analogous phenotypes in vivo.
source: As expected from the reduced in vitro growth phenotype in HFFs and BMDMs, ΔMYR1-Luc showed reduced bioluminescent signal compared to WT-Luc parasites (Figure 2b and c), confirming that the growth defect in vitro results in analogous phenotypes in vivo.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of in vitro and in vivo data.

claim: MYR1-deficient parasites were able to expand in mice, as bioluminescence signal increased from day 3 to day 5 post infection.
source: Nevertheless, MYR1-deficient parasites were still able to expand in mice, as bioluminescence signal increased from day 3 to day 5 post infection (Figure 2b and c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b and c.

claim: The initial increase of growth of ΔMYR1 parasites is similar to what was observed for ΔIST parasites.
source: This initial increase of growth is similar to what was observed for ΔIST parasites (Olias et al., 2016; Gay et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: ΔMYR1-Luc-infected mice that survived the acute phase of infection for 4 weeks p.i. carried a low number of cysts in the brain (3.4 cysts/brain on average; 0–13 cysts/brain detected).
source: ΔMYR1-Luc-infected mice that survived the acute phase of infection for 4 weeks p.i. carried a low number of cysts in the brain (3.4 cysts/brain on average; 0–13 cysts/brain detected, Figure 2d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Expression of luciferase does not decrease the ability of ΔMYR1 parasites to produce cysts.
source: This is similar to previous observations (Young et al., 2019) indicating that expression of luciferase does not decrease the ability to produce cysts and further supports the notion that ΔMYR1 parasites are able to form cysts, albeit at low numbers.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison with prior observations.

claim: ΔMYR1 parasites are able to form cysts, albeit at low numbers.
source: This is similar to previous observations (Young et al., 2019) indicating that expression of luciferase does not decrease the ability to produce cysts and further supports the notion that ΔMYR1 parasites are able to form cysts, albeit at low numbers.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citation to prior work.

claim: ΔMYR1-Luc parasites proliferate better in mice co-infected with WT parasites than with ΔMYR1 parasites.
source: Our results show that ΔMYR1-Luc parasites proliferate better in mice co-infected with WT parasites than with ΔMYR1 parasites (Figure 3b and c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3b and c.

claim: The results support a paracrine role of MYR1-mediated effectors in vivo.
source: These results support a paracrine role of MYR1-mediated effectors in vivo (Figure 4).
evidence: This is inferred from the co-infection experimental data.

claim: Mice infected with a mix of ΔMYR1:WT or ΔMYR1:ΔMYR1 parasites display comparable levels of IL-12p40 in both peritoneum and serum at day 7 p.i.
source: Mice infected with a mix of ΔMYR1:WT or ΔMYR1:ΔMYR1 parasites display comparable levels of IL-12p40 in both peritoneum and serum at day 7 p.i.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from ELISA measurements.

claim: ΔMYR1:WT infections elicited higher levels of CCL2/MCP-1, TNF and IFN-γ compared to the ΔMYR1:ΔMYR1 mix.
source: However, ΔMYR1:WT infections elicited higher levels of CCL2/MCP-1, TNF and especially IFN-γ compared to the ΔMYR1:ΔMYR1 mix (Figure 3d, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3d and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: ΔMYR1-Luc growth is rescued even when high levels of IFN-γ are produced in the peritoneal cavity.
source: Considering that ΔMYR1-Luc growth is rescued even when high levels of IFN-γ are produced in the peritoneal cavity, we wanted to assess whether disrupting IFN-γ-producing cell populations would impact the trans-rescue phenotype.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing rescue despite high IFN-γ levels.

claim: Lymphocytes, in particular CD8+, Th1-committed CD4+ and γδ T cells, are the main sources of IFN-γ during Toxoplasma infection.
source: Lymphocytes, in particular CD8+, Th1-committed CD4+ and γδ T cells, are the main sources of IFN-γ during Toxoplasma infection (Nishiyama et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Rag2-deficient mice do not produce mature T and B cells.
source: Thus, we applied the same mixed infection strategy in Rag2-deficient mice that do not produce mature T and B cells, and therefore fail to deploy adaptive immune responses (Shinkai et al., 1992; Figure 3e).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Rag2-deficient mice fail to deploy adaptive immune responses.
source: Thus, we applied the same mixed infection strategy in Rag2-deficient mice that do not produce mature T and B cells, and therefore fail to deploy adaptive immune responses (Shinkai et al., 1992; Figure 3e).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: An overall higher parasitaemia was detected in Rag2-/- mice when compared to WT mice.
source: As expected, an overall higher parasitaemia was detected in Rag2-/- mice when compared to WT mice, due to the known role of the T and B cells to control infection.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and established knowledge.

claim: In both Rag2-/- and WT control mice ΔMYR1-Luc parasites proliferate more when mixed with WT parasites than with ΔMYR1 parasites.
source: Nevertheless, in both Rag2-/- and WT control mice ΔMYR1-Luc parasites proliferate more when mixed with WT parasites than with ΔMYR1 parasites (Figure 3f).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3f.

claim: The host adaptive response is not essential for the trans-rescue of MYR1-deficient Toxoplasma during acute infection.
source: These results confirm that the host adaptive response is not essential for the trans-rescue of MYR1-deficient Toxoplasma during acute infection.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data in Rag2-/- mice.

claim: Deletion of MYR1, and by extension MYR1-dependent effectors, does not impact the ability of Toxoplasma to initiate an infection in mice.
source: In this work, we show that deletion of MYR1, and by extension MYR1-dependent effectors, does not impact the ability of Toxoplasma to initiate an infection in mice and survive in IFN-γ-stimulated murine macrophages.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Deletion of MYR1, and by extension MYR1-dependent effectors, does not impact the ability of Toxoplasma to survive in IFN-γ-stimulated murine macrophages.
source: In this work, we show that deletion of MYR1, and by extension MYR1-dependent effectors, does not impact the ability of Toxoplasma to initiate an infection in mice and survive in IFN-γ-stimulated murine macrophages.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Clonal ΔMYR1 mutants have a significantly reduced growth compared to WT parasites in vivo.
source: While clonal ΔMYR1 mutants have a significantly reduced growth compared to WT parasites in vivo, co-infection with WT parasites increased their ability to proliferate.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Co-infection with WT parasites increased the ability of ΔMYR1 mutants to proliferate.
source: While clonal ΔMYR1 mutants have a significantly reduced growth compared to WT parasites in vivo, co-infection with WT parasites increased their ability to proliferate.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Loss-of-function mutants of Myr1 and other genes involved in PV translocation of effector proteins show no or only relatively minor fitness defects in mice in pooled CRISPR-Cas9 screens.
source: This finding supports results from pooled CRISPR-Cas9 screens, where loss-of-function mutants of Myr1 and other genes previously shown to be involved in PV translocation of effector proteins, show no (Young et al., 2019; Butterworth et al., 2022; Sangaré et al., 2019; Tachibana et al., 2023) or only relatively minor fitness defects in mice (Giuliano et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The rescue phenotype observed in mixed infections is very unlikely to occur through co-infection of host cells by WT and ΔMYR1 parasites.
source: The rescue phenotype observed in mixed infections is very unlikely to occur through co-infection of host cells by WT and ΔMYR1 parasites, as in the peritoneal exudate from infected mice less than 2% of all infected cells were co-infected (data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data (not shown in the manuscript).

claim: Less than 2% of all infected cells in the peritoneal exudate from infected mice were co-infected.
source: The rescue phenotype observed in mixed infections is very unlikely to occur through co-infection of host cells by WT and ΔMYR1 parasites, as in the peritoneal exudate from infected mice less than 2% of all infected cells were co-infected (data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data (not shown in the manuscript).

claim: Some MYR1-dependent effectors cause changes in infected murine cells, that in turn provide a favourable environment for parasite growth in a paracrine manner.
source: As such, our data indicates that some MYR1-dependent effectors cause changes in infected murine cells, that in turn provide a favourable environment for parasite growth in a paracrine manner (Figure 4).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data.

claim: The major transcriptional changes caused by MYR-dependent effectors are not required for Toxoplasma to survive cell-autonomous immune responses in IFN-γ-primed cells.
source: This is important as: (1) it shows that the major transcriptional changes caused by MYR-dependent effectors are not required for Toxoplasma to survive cell-autonomous immune responses in IFN-γ-primed cells; (2) Paracrine rescue in pooled CRISPR-Cas9 screens may mask a significant amount of proteins required for Toxoplasma survival; (3) It is likely that this 'paracrine masking effect' can be found in CRISPR screens in other biological contexts, for example: other host-microbe interaction screens, and possibly even in non-infectious biological contexts, such as pooled CRISPR screen approaches to study cancer immunity and to discover regulators of innate and adaptive immunity crosstalk (reviewed in Shi et al., 2023; Holcomb et al., 2022).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data.

claim: Paracrine rescue in pooled CRISPR-Cas9 screens may mask a significant amount of proteins required for Toxoplasma survival.
source: This is important as: (1) it shows that the major transcriptional changes caused by MYR-dependent effectors are not required for Toxoplasma to survive cell-autonomous immune responses in IFN-γ-primed cells; (2) Paracrine rescue in pooled CRISPR-Cas9 screens may mask a significant amount of proteins required for Toxoplasma survival; (3) It is likely that this 'paracrine masking effect' can be found in CRISPR screens in other biological contexts, for example: other host-microbe interaction screens, and possibly even in non-infectious biological contexts, such as pooled CRISPR screen approaches to study cancer immunity and to discover regulators of innate and adaptive immunity crosstalk (reviewed in Shi et al., 2023; Holcomb et al., 2022).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data.

claim: The 'paracrine masking effect' can likely be found in CRISPR screens in other biological contexts.
source: This is important as: (1) it shows that the major transcriptional changes caused by MYR-dependent effectors are not required for Toxoplasma to survive cell-autonomous immune responses in IFN-γ-primed cells; (2) Paracrine rescue in pooled CRISPR-Cas9 screens may mask a significant amount of proteins required for Toxoplasma survival; (3) It is likely that this 'paracrine masking effect' can be found in CRISPR screens in other biological contexts, for example: other host-microbe interaction screens, and possibly even in non-infectious biological contexts, such as pooled CRISPR screen approaches to study cancer immunity and to discover regulators of innate and adaptive immunity crosstalk (reviewed in Shi et al., 2023; Holcomb et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the findings.

claim: The presence of WT parasites in a mixed inoculum with ΔMYR1 mutants elicited significantly higher levels of IFN-γ and TNF in the peritoneum than ΔMYR1 mutants alone.
source: We found that the presence of WT parasites in a mixed inoculum with ΔMYR1 mutants elicited significantly higher levels of IFN-γ and TNF in the peritoneum than ΔMYR1 mutants alone.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from ELISA measurements.

claim: IFN-γ is a major cytokine to limit Toxoplasma growth in a cell-autonomous manner.
source: As IFN-γ was shown to be a major cytokine to limit Toxoplasma growth in a cell-autonomous manner, and that TNF acts mainly by enhancing the antimicrobial effects in IFN-γ-activated cells, one would expect that ΔMYR1-Luc parasites would be more restricted when injected in combination with WT parasites.
evidence: This is established knowledge about IFN-γ function.

claim: TNF acts mainly by enhancing the antimicrobial effects in IFN-γ-activated cells.
source: As IFN-γ was shown to be a major cytokine to limit Toxoplasma growth in a cell-autonomous manner, and that TNF acts mainly by enhancing the antimicrobial effects in IFN-γ-activated cells, one would expect that ΔMYR1-Luc parasites would be more restricted when injected in combination with WT parasites.
evidence: This is established knowledge about TNF function.

claim: Higher ΔMYR1-Luc parasitaemia was observed in ΔMYR1:WT than in ΔMYR1:ΔMYR1 mixes.
source: However, we observed the opposite, as higher ΔMYR1-Luc parasitaemia was observed in ΔMYR1:WT than in ΔMYR1:ΔMYR1 mixes.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: MYR1, and by extension MYR1-dependent effectors, do not protect Toxoplasma from the IFN-γ-mediated intracellular clearance in mice.
source: These data provide further support that MYR1, and by extension MYR1-dependent effectors, do not protect Toxoplasma from the IFN-γ-mediated intracellular clearance in mice.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing rescue despite high IFN-γ levels.

claim: The adaptive immune system plays no role in the rescue of ΔMYR1 parasites by WT parasites.
source: We show that the adaptive immune system plays no role, pointing towards cells of the innate immune system.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Rag2-/- mice.

claim: Higher CCL2 levels in mice infected with ΔMYR1:WT suggests higher inflammatory Ly6Chigh monocytes recruitment to infected tissues.
source: Higher CCL2 levels in mice infected with ΔMYR1:WT suggests higher inflammatory Ly6Chigh monocytes recruitment to infected tissues (Robben et al., 2005; Dunay et al., 2008).
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Recruited monocytes could be responsible for the high levels of TNF and IFN-γ detected.
source: These cells could be responsible for the high levels of TNF and IFN-γ detected.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the data.

claim: Monocytes have been shown to be important for limiting Toxoplasma upon exposure to IFN-γ in infected niches.
source: While monocytes have been shown in multiple reports to be important for limiting Toxoplasma upon exposure to IFN-γ in infected niches (Robben et al., 2005; Goldszmid et al., 2012; Mordue and Sibley, 2003), it is possible that recruited monocytes also provide an important reservoir for parasites to grow in the peritoneum.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: It is possible that recruited monocytes also provide an important reservoir for parasites to grow in the peritoneum.
source: While monocytes have been shown in multiple reports to be important for limiting Toxoplasma upon exposure to IFN-γ in infected niches (Robben et al., 2005; Goldszmid et al., 2012; Mordue and Sibley, 2003), it is possible that recruited monocytes also provide an important reservoir for parasites to grow in the peritoneum.
evidence: This is a speculative inference.

claim: The paracrine rescue phenotype is likely the concerted result of multiple effectors that affect cytokine secretion.
source: Individual MYR-related effectors that may be responsible for the paracrine rescue have not been investigated here and we hypothesise that the phenotype is likely the concerted result of multiple effectors that affect cytokine secretion.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the findings.

claim: Both GRA18 and GRA28 can induce release of CCL22 from infected cells.
source: For example, previous studies showed that both GRA18 and GRA28 can induce release of CCL22 from infected cells (He et al., 2018; Rudzki et al., 2021), while GRA16 and HCE1/TEEGR impair NF-kB signalling and the potential release of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6, IL-1β, and TNF (Braun et al., 2019; Seo et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: GRA16 and HCE1/TEEGR impair NF-kB signalling and the potential release of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6, IL-1β, and TNF.
source: For example, previous studies showed that both GRA18 and GRA28 can induce release of CCL22 from infected cells (He et al., 2018; Rudzki et al., 2021), while GRA16 and HCE1/TEEGR impair NF-kB signalling and the potential release of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6, IL-1β, and TNF (Braun et al., 2019; Seo et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: MYR1-dependent effectors establish a supportive environment in trans for Toxoplasma growth within the peritoneum.
source: Regardless of the effector(s), our results highlight an important novel function of MYR1-dependent effectors by establishing a supportive environment in trans for Toxoplasma growth within the peritoneum.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data.

claim: MYR1 appears to be dispensable for the formation and persistence of latent Toxoplasma stages per se.
source: We further confirm previous results using luciferase-expressing ΔMYR1 parasites that MYR1 appears to be dispensable for the formation and persistence of latent Toxoplasma stages per se.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citation to prior work.

claim: MYR1 has been demonstrated to be dispensable for stage conversion in vitro.
source: As MYR1 has been demonstrated to be dispensable for stage conversion in vitro (Seizova et al., 2022), the relatively low number of cysts is likely explained by a failure of ΔMYR1 parasites to efficiently disseminate and/or persist within the murine host (Ten Hoeve et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The relatively low number of cysts is likely explained by a failure of ΔMYR1 parasites to efficiently disseminate and/or persist within the murine host.
source: As MYR1 has been demonstrated to be dispensable for stage conversion in vitro (Seizova et al., 2022), the relatively low number of cysts is likely explained by a failure of ΔMYR1 parasites to efficiently disseminate and/or persist within the murine host (Ten Hoeve et al., 2022).
evidence: This is inferred from the data and supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The absence of CCL2 in ΔMYR1 infections may limit recruitment of host cells that Toxoplasma can potentially use as vehicles to reach the brain.
source: In alternative, we hypothesise that the absence of CCL2 in ΔMYR1 infections limits recruitment of host cells that Toxoplasma can potentially use as vehicles to reach the brain.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the findings.

claim: Novel applications of CRISPR screens, for example in combination with single-cell RNA sequencing or with functional assays to explore immunological contexts, could help understand how infected cells affect the neighbouring environment to support infection.
source: Novel applications of the CRISPR screens, for example in combination with single-cell RNA sequencing (Butterworth et al., 2023) or with functional assays to explore immunological contexts (Shi et al., 2023) could help understand how infected cells affect the neighbouring environment to support infection, and contribute to parasite survival, dissemination and persistence within the host.
evidence: This is a speculative suggestion for future research.

claim: MYR1-dependent proteins play a critical role in promoting a favourable environment for growth beyond the infected cell in a paracrine manner.
source: Here, we show that MYR1-dependent proteins play a critical role in promoting a favourable environment for growth beyond the infected cell in a paracrine manner.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The paracrine function of MYR1-dependent proteins is different to the injection of rhoptry effector proteins by Toxoplasma into cells it does not invade, which requires parasite-host cell contact.
source: This is different to the injection of rhoptry effector proteins by Toxoplasma into cells it does not invade, which requires parasite-host cell contact (Koshy et al., 2012), and provides a novel angle on how the parasite can systematically alter the host environment in its favour during infection.
evidence: This is inferred from the data and supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Toxoplasma can inject rhoptry effector proteins into cells it does not invade, which requires parasite-host cell contact.
source: This is different to the injection of rhoptry effector proteins by Toxoplasma into cells it does not invade, which requires parasite-host cell contact (Koshy et al., 2012), and provides a novel angle on how the parasite can systematically alter the host environment in its favour during infection.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The limitation that mutant phenotypes can be masked in pooled CRISPR screens likely extends to other experimental setups where paracrine effects are possible.
source: The limitation we highlight here, that mutant phenotypes can be masked in pooled CRISPR screens, likely extends to other experimental setups where paracrine effects are possible.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the findings.
